faq.q: How do I calculate projector screen size for an event?
faq.a: Measure from the screen to the farthest seat. For general content like video and big slides, make the image height about one sixth of that distance; for detailed spreadsheets or small text, aim for about one quarter.

faq.q: How many lumens do I need for a projector at a conference?
faq.a: As a rule of thumb, a 10 to 12 ft wide screen in a normally lit ballroom needs roughly 5,000 to 7,000 lumens. Bright spaces with daylight or large screens over 16 ft wide usually need more output or multiple projectors.

faq.q: What is a good throw ratio for event projection?
faq.a: Standard lenses sit around 1.3:1 to 2.0:1, which suits most ballrooms with a projector at the back or on truss. Short-throw lenses (under about 0.8:1) work when there is little space, and long-throw lenses help when the projector must sit far back.

faq.q: Is rear projection better than front projection?
faq.a: Rear projection hides the projector and avoids presenter shadows, but it needs clear space behind the screen equal to the throw distance. Front projection uses less floor space and is easier to fit in most venues.

faq.q: Should I use 16:9 or 16:10 for my presentation?
faq.a: Match the screen to your content. Most video and modern slide decks are 16:9; many laptops and laser projectors are natively 16:10, so set the output to 16:9 if that is how the deck was built.

body:
Short answer: Pick your projector screen size from the farthest viewer: as a rule of thumb, make the image height about 1/6 of the distance to the back row for video and big slides, or about 1/4 for detailed content like spreadsheets. Then choose lumens by screen size and ambient light. A 10 ft wide screen in a normally lit event space typically needs around 5,000 lumens; daylight or screens over 16 ft wide need more output or blended projectors.

[[IMAGE]]

This guide covers screen sizing, aspect ratio, throw distance, how many lumens you need, screen types, edge blending and content resolution, with worked examples you can use for planning.

How to choose projector screen size from the farthest viewer

The most reliable way to size a screen is to work backward from the last row. Measure from where the screen will stand to the farthest seat, then apply one of two common rules of thumb:

  • General content (1/6 rule) — video, photos, large-type keynote slides. Image height is about 1/6 of the farthest viewing distance.
  • Detailed content (1/4 rule) — spreadsheets, charts with small labels, code, dense slides. Image height is about 1/4 of the farthest viewing distance.

Once you have the height, the aspect ratio gives you the width. Also check the bottom of the image: it should sit at least 4 to 5 ft off the floor so heads in the front rows do not block it. In New York lofts and hotel ballrooms with low beams, that often sets the maximum screen height.

Aspect ratio: 16:9 vs 16:10 vs 4:3

  • 16:9 — the standard for video, streaming and most current slide templates. Width is about 1.78 times the height.
  • 16:10 — native on many laptops and laser projectors (1920 x 1200). Width is 1.6 times the height. Good for presenters who show their desktop.
  • 4:3 — older decks and some legacy content. Width is 1.33 times the height. Rare for events now.

Build the screen and the content to the same ratio. If your deck is 16:9 and the screen is 16:10, you get black bars, which is fine; the reverse wastes the edges of your content.

Worked examples: audience depth to screen size and lumens

These figures use a 16:9 screen and are rounded to common screen sizes.

Farthest viewerGeneral content (1/6 rule), H x WDetailed content (1/4 rule), H x WTypical lumens, normal light
24 ft (small meeting, 30-50 seats)4 ft x 7 ft6 ft x 10.5 ft3,000-5,000
36 ft (breakout or board event, 60-100 seats)6 ft x 10.5 ft9 ft x 16 ft5,000-7,000
48 ft (mid-size conference, 120-200 seats)8 ft x 14 ft12 ft x 21 ft7,000, or two blended
60 ft (gala or ballroom, 250-400 seats)10 ft x 18 ft15 ft x 27 ft7,000+ per projector, often blended
90 ft+ (large general session)15 ft x 27 ft22 ft x 40 ftMultiple blended projectors

Once a single screen passes about 16 to 20 ft wide, most planners switch to two or more blended projectors or split content across left and right screens.

How many lumens do I need for a projector?

Brightness depends on two things: how big the image is and how much light hits it. The same projector looks bright on an 8 ft screen and washed out on a 20 ft one. Typical ranges for a projector lumens target at an event:

  • Dim (house lights down, no windows) — about 2,000 to 3,000 lumens for screens up to 8 ft wide; 4,000 to 5,000 for 10 to 12 ft.
  • Normal (house lights up for note taking) — about 3,500 to 5,000 lumens for up to 8 ft wide; 5,000 to 7,000 for 10 to 14 ft.
  • Bright or daylight (glass walls, atriums, outdoor dusk) — 7,000 lumens and up, often with stacked or blended projectors and a high-gain screen.

Control the light first: keep stage wash off the screen and dim fixtures directly over it. That often does more than an extra 1,000 lumens.

Throw distance and throw ratio

Throw ratio tells you how far the projector must be from the screen: throw distance = throw ratio x image width. A 1.5:1 lens filling a 12 ft wide screen sits about 18 ft back.

  • Short throw (about 0.4:1 to 0.8:1) — projector sits close to the screen. Useful for tight spaces and rear projection with little backstage depth.
  • Standard (about 1.3:1 to 2.0:1) — the usual choice for ballrooms and conference spaces, with the projector on a riser, a tech table or hung on truss.
  • Long throw (about 2.5:1 and up) — projector at the back of a deep space or in a booth, keeping it clear of sightlines.

Projectors can be hung from the ceiling or from truss with proper clamps and safety cables, which keeps them out of the audience and away from bumps.

Front vs rear projection

Front projection places the projector on the audience side. It is simpler, uses less floor space and works with almost any screen. The trade-off is presenter shadows if someone walks into the beam.

Rear projection places the projector behind a translucent screen. The look is cleaner and presenters cast no shadows. You need clear space behind the screen equal to the throw distance, or a short-throw lens or mirror to cut it down.

Screen types for events

  • Fast-fold screens — an aluminum frame with a snap-on front or rear surface and optional drape kit. Common 16:9 sizes run from roughly 6 x 10.5 ft up to 9 x 16 ft and beyond. The standard for conferences and galas.
  • Tripod screens — quick to set, best for small meetings and breakouts with screens up to about 8 ft wide.
  • Truss-mounted screens — screen surfaces framed into or hung from truss, often for large widescreen setups, stage backdrops and custom shapes.
  • Any surface — walls, facades, sculptures and set pieces can be the screen with projection mapping. See our projection mapping guide.

Edge blending for wide screens

When you want one very wide image, two or more projectors overlap by roughly 15 to 20 percent and the overlap is softened in software or in the projector so it reads as one picture. Blending also adds brightness across a large surface. It needs matched projectors, careful alignment and a processor that outputs the full canvas.

Laptop and content resolution

  • Match native resolution — many laser projectors are WUXGA (1920 x 1200). Build content at 1920 x 1080 for 16:9 or 1920 x 1200 for 16:10.
  • Blended canvases — a two-projector blend may need a custom width, for example around 3,500 pixels. Confirm the exact canvas before designing.
  • Signal over distance — long HDMI runs fail. Use HDBaseT, SDI or fiber extenders from the stage to the projector.
  • Presenter setup — test with the actual laptop, set it to extend or mirror as needed, and bring the right adapters.

When an LED wall makes more sense

For daylight, outdoor events or very bright stages, an LED wall can beat projection; compare both in projector vs LED wall. LED walls are rented through our sister site ledwall.nyc.
